title: The Last Man on Earth

evidence.note: The two Internet Archive items carry different labels. TheLastManOnEarth_72 has a CC0 1.0 license URL and its metadata says 'In the Public Domain'. TheLastManOnEarthHD has a Public Domain Mark 1.0 license URL (checked in the items' metadata). Both are uploader labels, not rights determinations. The film was released in 1964. Cornell's public domain guide lists works published 1964-1977 with proper notice as protected for 95 years from publication, with no renewal step needed. A missed renewal therefore cannot by itself have put a 1964 US film into the public domain. Any public domain status would have to rest on a failure of the copyright notice, and no document establishing that was located. The common online claim that the film was lost through a failure to renew is not supported by this reading.
evidence.source: Cornell University Library — Copyright & Fair Use: Public Domain

evidence.note: The film is an Italian-American co-production. The URAA restored US copyright in foreign works that had fallen into the US public domain through a failure to comply with US formalities, as of 1 January 1996. Whether this film is an eligible foreign work, and what its Italian term was, was not verified, so the restoration question is unresolved.
evidence.source: Cornell University Library — Copyright & Fair Use: Public Domain (URAA section)

evidence.note: This is a sound film, and its recorded track normally shares the film print's copyright status, so the score layer follows the unresolved print layer. No separate score registration was located.

The Internet Archive metadata for the film says it is based on Richard Matheson's novel "I am Legend". The novel is a separate work that is treated as still protected. Under Stewart v. Abend, distributing a derivative work during the renewal term of the underlying work infringes the owner's rights unless the owner consents. The source story can therefore restrict reuse of the film whatever the print's status. The novel's registration and renewal records were not pulled.
evidence.source: Stewart v. Abend, 495 U.S. 207 (1990) — Cornell Law School Legal Information Institute

evidence.note: No trademark registration for the title or related franchise names was checked. The source novel has been adapted commercially more than once, so avoid franchise naming in titles or branding.

A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright: copying or restoring public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). What a restoration ADDS can be protected: a newly composed or newly recorded score, colorization, newly written or translated titles and subtitles, and other original additions. Separately, ripping a copy-protected Blu-ray or DVD can break the DMCA's anti-circumvention rule (17 U.S.C. 1201) even when the film itself is public domain.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp. (summary)

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. 1201 - circumvention of copyright protection systems.
The Internet Archive HD item's metadata describes the upload as an HD restoration. Modern HD remasters can carry new protectable elements.

editorial:
The Last Man on Earth (1964) is a horror film starring Vincent Price as Dr. Robert Morgan, the only healthy survivor of a plague that has turned the rest of humanity into night-dwelling creatures. Franca Bettoia and Giacomo Rossi Stuart also appear. The Internet Archive metadata credits Ubaldo Ragona as director, lists Robert L. Lippert as creator, and says it is based on Richard Matheson's novel "I am Legend". Two Internet Archive items host it, with different free-use labels: CC0 1.0 on one and Public Domain Mark 1.0 on the other.

The rights trap has two parts. First, the print's free status is unconfirmed. Those labels are uploader designations. Works published from 1964 to 1977 with proper notice are protected for 95 years without renewal, so the popular explanation that the film lapsed through a missed renewal does not hold up. Any public domain claim would have to rest on a notice failure that this research did not document. The Italian-American co-production origin also leaves a possible URAA restoration question open. Second, Matheson's novel is a separate work still treated as protected. Under Stewart v. Abend, a new commercial adaptation or reuse of the story can require a license from the novel's owner even if the print itself were free.
faq: The film is hosted everywhere as public domain. Is that confirmed?

No. The Internet Archive's CC0 and Public Domain Mark labels are uploader designations. Works published 1964–1977 with notice are protected for 95 years without a renewal filing, so a missed renewal is not a route to public domain here. Only a failure of the copyright notice could be, and this research found no record showing that. The Italian-American co-production origin also leaves a URAA restoration claim unresolved.
Can I make a new adaptation based on this film?

Not without clearing the underlying novel. Richard Matheson's I Am Legend is a separate protected work. Under Stewart v. Abend, its owner can restrict distribution of a derivative film even if the film print is free to use.
